I'll be honest, Eduarda. I'm hesitant. Two other banks were here this week.
I understand. So let me start with a question. What would happen to Lane Packaging if you retired tomorrow?
Honestly? I don't know. My son works in tech. He doesn't want to run a factory.
Then wouldn't you agree that this is the right moment to plan? Our value proposition is simple: the right buyer, not just the highest price.

Hi Eduarda, it's James. Some thoughts before your pitch to Victor Lane tomorrow. Remember, he is hesitant. He built Lane Packaging over thirty years, and selling it is emotional for him. So don't start with numbers. Start with a question he cannot ignore: what would happen to the company if he retired tomorrow? Then give him our value proposition in one sentence. Our credibility comes from the deals we closed in packaging last year, so mention two of them. And close with a question too: why not find out what the business is really worth? If you win him over, we get the mandate. Good luck.

Why do the best pitches use so many questions? Because a question makes the listener think, and a statement only asks them to agree. When you say, wouldn't you agree that timing matters, the client answers yes in their head. That small yes builds buy-in. Rhetorical questions do not need an answer. They guide the listener to the answer you want. But use them carefully. Three or four in a pitch is enough. More than that and you come across as a salesperson, not an advisor. Ask the question, pause, and let the silence work for you.

Eduarda met Victor Lane, the hesitant founder of Lane Packaging. She opened the pitch with a question: what would happen to the company if he retired tomorrow? Then she gave him her value proposition in one sentence. She built credibility with two packaging deals her team closed last year. Victor still had doubts, so she asked: why not test the market now? In the end, she won him over and got the mandate.
